blocks.text: I can find the inverse of a function.

items.title: Finding the inverse of a function
The graphs of functions and their inverse

blocks.text: Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: A function is a mathematical relationship that uniquely maps values of one set to the values of another set.
The domain of a function is the set of values that the mapping is performed on.
The range of a function is the set of values mapped to by the function and the stated domain.
An inverse function reverses the mapping of the original function.

blocks.text: For f(x) = 5x, the values of the domain (x) are mapped onto the values of the range (f(x)) by multiplying by 5. For example, f(−1) = −5, f(0) = 0, f(1) = 5 and f(2) = 10.
Sometimes we need to map values of the range back to the domain. If f(x) = 20, what value of x mapped to 20?
The same works for 75 and −40: x = 75 ÷ 5 = 15 and x = −40 ÷ 5 = −8. Each time we divide by 5 to map back from the range to the domain.
To map any f(x) value back we can use x = f(x) ÷ 5. This is known as the {inverse function}, as it reverses the mapping.
We write it using this notation: f⁻¹(x) = x ÷ 5, or f⁻¹(x) = x/5.

items: A function maps values of the domain to values in the range.
The inverse function maps values of the range back to values in the domain.
The range of a function is the domain of its inverse function.

blocks.text: Andeep says: “With exponents, x to the power of −1 equals 1/x. Doesn’t that mean f⁻¹(x) equals 1/f(x)?”

blocks.label: Sam’s answer
blocks.text: No. This is function notation. f⁻¹(x) means “f inverse of x”. We have seen an example like this before: sin⁻¹(x) is “sine inverse of x”.
For f(x) = x + 10 the inverse function is f⁻¹(x) = x − 10. We say it aloud as “f inverse of x equals x minus 10”.

blocks.q: Choose the inverse function f⁻¹(x) of each function.

blocks.text: We can check that an inverse function is correct by substituting a value into the original function.
f(x) = 12x maps 4 to 48. Does the inverse function f⁻¹(x) = x/12 map 48 back to 4?
It does, so we know we are correct: the inverse function reverses the mapping. Another example: f(x) = x + 15 has inverse f⁻¹(x) = x − 15, and f(7) = 22 while f⁻¹(22) = 22 − 15 = 7.
Functions with several steps still have an inverse. We find it by making x the subject.
f(x) = 2x + 1. Subtract 1 from both sides: f(x) − 1 = 2x. Then divide both sides by 2:
x = (f(x) − 1)/2, so the inverse function is “subtract 1, then divide by 2”: f⁻¹(x) = (x − 1)/2.
Check it works: f(8) = 2(8) + 1 = 17, and f⁻¹(17) = (17 − 1)/2 = 8. The inverse function has reversed the mapping from 17 back to 8.
Now try f(x) = (x − 1)/2. To map f(x) back to the original x we must “multiply by 2, then add 1”.
Check: f(9) = (9 − 1)/2 = 4, and f⁻¹(4) = 2(4) + 1 = 9. The inverse function reverses the mapping.

blocks.q: Which is the inverse function f⁻¹(x)?

blocks.text: The function f(x) = x/3 + 2 maps 12 to 6. Which candidate inverse maps 6 back to 12?

blocks.why: 3(6 − 2) = 12, so it maps 6 back to 12. The other two give 16 and 0.

slides.title: Graphs of a function and its inverse

blocks.text: Look at f(x) = 2x and its inverse f⁻¹(x) = x/2. The function maps 1 to 2, 2 to 4, 3 to 6 and 4 to 8. The inverse maps 2 to 1, 4 to 2, 6 to 3 and 8 to 4.

blocks.label: What do you notice?
blocks.text: Because the inverse function reverses the mapping, the x coordinate has become the y coordinate and vice versa.
The graph of the inverse function is a {reflection} of the original function in the line y = x.
Look at tables of values for f(x) and f⁻¹(x). The domain of the original function is the range of the inverse function, and the range of the original function is the domain of the inverse function.
For example, f(x) = 4x − 1 has inverse f⁻¹(x) = (x + 1)/4. Since f(2) = 7 and f(3) = 11, we get f⁻¹(7) = 2 and f⁻¹(11) = 3.

items.q: The point (3, 12) is on the graph of f. Which point is on the graph of f⁻¹?
The domain of f becomes the ___ of f⁻¹.

slides.title: When an inverse needs a restriction

blocks.text: If we reflect a many-to-one function such as f(x) = x² in the line y = x, we create a one-to-many relationship. That is not a valid function.
We can get round this by restricting the domain of the original function, for example f(x) = x² where x is greater than or equal to 0. Then it is one-to-one and the inverse function is f⁻¹(x) = √x.

blocks.q: Why can the inverse of f(x) = x² (for all x) not be a valid function?
options: Reflecting it in y = x gives a one-to-many relationship
Its domain is the same as its range
It does not have a graph
blocks.why: One input would map to many outputs, so the reflection is not a valid function. Restricting the domain fixes it.

blocks.q: Which of these functions need their domain restricted so that the inverse is valid?
columns: Inverse is valid as it stands (one-to-one)

slides.title: Finding the inverse of a function

items: The inverse of a function can be found by rearranging to make x the subject.
The inverse function reverses the mapping of the original function.
The graph of the inverse function is a reflection in the line y = x.
Not all functions have an inverse function as the inverse may be a one-to-many relationship, but it may be possible to restrict the domain to make the inverse function valid.

flashcards.back: A function that reverses the mapping of the original function.
“f inverse of x”. It is function notation and does not mean 1/f(x).

flashcards.front: What is the inverse of f(x) = 9x?
What is the inverse of f(x) = x + 10?
How do you find the inverse of a multi-step function?
flashcards.back: Make x the subject (rearrange the function).

flashcards.front: How can you check that an inverse function is correct?
flashcards.back:
Put a value into f, then put the output into f⁻¹. You should get back to the value you started with.

Example: f(x) = 12x, f(4) = 48 and f⁻¹(48) = 4.

flashcards.front: The range of a function is the ___ of its inverse function.
How are the graphs of f and f⁻¹ related?
flashcards.back: They are reflections of each other in the line y = x.

flashcards.front: The point (2, 4) is on the graph of f. What point is on the graph of f⁻¹?
flashcards.back: (4, 2): the x and y coordinates swap.

flashcards.front: Why does f(x) = x² need a restricted domain to have a valid inverse?
flashcards.back:
It is many-to-one, so its reflection is one-to-many, which is not a valid function.

With x greater than or equal to 0 the inverse is f⁻¹(x) = √x.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Finding the inverse of a function
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a number, a word, or y = x where asked.

questions.prompt: f(x) = 6x − 5. What value of x maps to 37?
f(x) = 4x − 1, so f⁻¹(x) = (x + 1)/4. What is f⁻¹(15)?
f(x) = x/7 + 4, so f⁻¹(x) = 7(x − 4). What is f⁻¹(25)?
The point (3, 12) is on the graph of y = f(x). What is the x coordinate of the matching point on the graph of y = f⁻¹(x)?
questions.explanation: The inverse reverses the mapping, so the coordinates swap: (12, 3).

questions.prompt: The graph of f⁻¹ is a reflection of the graph of f in which line? Write it as y = x.
questions.explanation: The graph of the inverse function is a reflection of the original function in the line y = x.

questions.prompt: f(x) = x², where x is greater than or equal to 0, has inverse f⁻¹(x) = √x. What is f⁻¹(49)?
The domain of f becomes the ___ of f⁻¹. Write the missing word.
questions.explanation: The domain of the original function is the range of the inverse function.

steps.title: Warm-up, goal and key words
doThis: Start with quick revision: substitute a value into a function, and rearrange an equation to make a letter the subject.
Read the goal together, then look at the four key words: function, domain, range, inverse function.
Ask what each key word means before showing the meaning.
steps.say: I can find the inverse of a function.

keywords.meaning: A function is a mathematical relationship that uniquely maps values of one set to the values of another set.
The domain of a function is the set of values that the mapping is performed on.
The range of a function is the set of values mapped to by the function and the stated domain.
An inverse function reverses the mapping of the original function.

checkFor.ask: For y = 7(x − 12), what is y when x = 6? And what is x when y = 35?
checkFor.lookFor: y = −42 when x = 6, and x = 17 when y = 35.

recap: Our goal: I can find the inverse of a function.
An inverse function reverses the mapping of the original function.

steps.title: Mapping forwards and mapping back
doThis: Show that f(x) = 5x maps values of the domain (x) onto values of the range (f(x)) by multiplying by 5, using a table of values.
Then ask a backwards question: if f(x) = 20, what value of x mapped to 20? Write 5x = 20 and solve the equation.
Point out that each time the student divided by 5 to map back from the range to the domain.
keyIdeas: A function maps values of the domain to values in the range.
Sometimes we need to map values of the range back to the domain.

checkFor.ask: For f(x) = 5x, what value of x mapped to 75?

recap: f(x) = 5x maps x to 5x by multiplying by 5.
To map back, divide by 5: if f(x) = 20 then x = 4.

steps.title: The inverse function, its notation and checking it
doThis: Explain that to map any f(x) value back we can use x = f(x) ÷ 5. This is the inverse function, because it reverses the mapping. It is written f⁻¹(x) = x ÷ 5, or f⁻¹(x) = x/5.
Explain that f⁻¹(x) is function notation and is said 'f inverse of x'. It does not mean 1 divided by f(x).
Show how to check an inverse: put a value into the original function, then put the answer into the inverse function. The inverse function must map it back to the value the student started with.
keyIdeas: The inverse function maps the output to the input.
The inverse function reverses the mapping of the original function.
The range of a function is the domain of its inverse function.
examples: f(x) = x + 10 has inverse f⁻¹(x) = x − 10, said 'f inverse of x equals x minus 10'.

checkFor.ask: What does f⁻¹(x) mean, and does it mean 1 divided by f(x)?
checkFor.lookFor: It means 'f inverse of x', the inverse function of f(x). It is function notation and does not mean 1 divided by f(x).

recap: The inverse function reverses the mapping: it maps the output back to the input.
f⁻¹(x) is said 'f inverse of x'.
Check by putting a value in, then putting the answer into the inverse. You should get the value you started with.

steps.title: Functions with more than one step
doThis: Explain that functions with several steps still have an inverse. Find it by making x the subject.
Work through f(x) = 2x + 1: subtract 1 from both sides, then divide both sides by 2.
Then work back the other way with f(x) = (x − 1)/2, and check both by substituting a value.
keyIdeas: By changing the subject, you can find the inverse function.
examples: f(x) = 2x + 1, so f(x) − 1 = 2x. The inverse is 'subtract 1 then divide by 2': f⁻¹(x) = (x − 1)/2.
f(x) = (x − 1)/2, so 2f(x) = x − 1 and 2f(x) + 1 = x. The inverse is 'multiply by 2 then add 1': f⁻¹(x) = 2x + 1.

checkFor.ask: How do you find the inverse of f(x) = 2x + 1?
checkFor.lookFor: Make x the subject: subtract 1 from f(x), then divide by 2, so f⁻¹(x) = (x − 1)/2.

recap: To find the inverse of a multi-step function, make x the subject.
For f(x) = 2x + 1 the inverse is 'subtract 1 then divide by 2'.
Always check by substituting a value.

steps.title: Graphs of a function and its inverse
doThis: Take f(x) = 2x and list the points it maps: 1 to 2, 2 to 4, 3 to 6 and 4 to 8. The inverse maps 2 to 1, 4 to 2, 6 to 3 and 8 to 4.

Ask what the student notices about the coordinates. The x coordinate has become the y coordinate and the other way round. Then draw the line y = x and show that the two sets of points are reflections of each other in it.
Show that the domain and range swap: the domain of the original function is the range of the inverse function, and the range of the original function is the domain of the inverse function.
keyIdeas: There is a graphical connection between a function and its inverse.
The graph of the inverse function is a reflection of the original function in the line y = x.
The domain of the original function is the range of the inverse function. The range of the original function is the domain of the inverse function.
examples: f(x) = 4x − 1: f(2) = 7 and f(3) = 11, so the inverse maps 7 to 2 and 11 to 3.

checkFor.ask: A function and its inverse are a reflection of each other in which line?

recap: The inverse function swaps x and y: (1, 2) becomes (2, 1).
The graph of an inverse function is a reflection in the line y = x.
The domain of a function becomes the range of its inverse, and the range becomes the domain.

steps.title: When an inverse needs a restricted domain
doThis: Show that reflecting a many-to-one function such as f(x) = x² in the line y = x gives a one-to-many relationship. One input maps to many outputs, so that is not a valid function.

Explain that the fix is to restrict the domain of the original function, for example f(x) = x² where x is greater than or equal to 0. Then the inverse function is valid and is still a reflection in the line y = x.
keyIdeas: Not all functions have an inverse function, as the inverse may be a one-to-many relationship.
It may be possible to restrict the domain to make the inverse function valid.

checkFor.ask: Why is the reflection of f(x) = x² in the line y = x not a valid function?
checkFor.lookFor: Reflecting a many-to-one function gives a one-to-many relationship, where one input maps to many outputs. Restricting the domain fixes it.

recap: Not every function has a valid inverse as it stands.
A one-to-many relationship is not a valid function.
Restricting the domain of the original function can fix it.

steps.title: Find and check inverses together
doThis: Give the student a function and ask them to make x the subject to find the inverse function.
Check each answer by substituting a value: the inverse function must map the output back to the input.
Then check a candidate inverse using a mapped pair of values, and say why an inverse that fails to map back is wrong.
examples: f(x) = x/3 + 2 maps 12 to 6. f⁻¹(x) = 3(x − 2) maps 6 back to 12, because 3(6 − 2) = 12.

checkFor.ask: How can you show that f⁻¹(x) = 3(x − 2) is the inverse of f(x) = x/3 + 2?
checkFor.lookFor: f(12) = 6, and f⁻¹(6) = 3(6 − 2) = 12, so the inverse maps the output back to the input.

recap: Make x the subject to find the inverse.
Then check it: the inverse must map the output back to the input.

steps.title: Try it on your own
doThis: Ask the student to do the lesson quiz on their own. It asks about the notation for an inverse function, finding the value of x that mapped to a given output, choosing and matching inverse functions, and the line of reflection.
Mark it together and talk through any answer they got wrong.
recap: Do the quiz questions on your own.
Look again at any you got wrong.

steps.title: Recap and finish
doThis: Ask the student to explain how to find an inverse function and what its graph looks like.

Finish with the summary: the inverse of a function can be found by making x the subject; the inverse function reverses the mapping, so its graph is a reflection in the line y = x; not all functions have an inverse function, but restricting the domain can make it valid.

checkFor.ask: How do you find the inverse of a function, and how are the two graphs connected?
checkFor.lookFor: Rearrange to make x the subject. The graph of the inverse function is a reflection of the original function in the line y = x.

recap: Can you do it now? I can find the inverse of a function.
Remember: make x the subject, and check by mapping back. The graphs are reflections in y = x.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pupils confuse the domain and the range when they think about the inverse function.
commonMistakes.fix: The range of a function is the domain of its inverse function. Use a table of values for both to show the swap.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pupils read f⁻¹(x) as 1 divided by f(x), because x to the power of −1 means 1 over x.
commonMistakes.fix: Explain that this is function notation. f⁻¹(x) is said 'f inverse of x' and means the inverse function, just as sin⁻¹(x) is 'sine inverse of x'.

watchOut: Get the student to check every inverse by substituting a value: the inverse function must reverse the mapping and give the starting value back.
When saying an inverse function aloud, say it in full, for example 'f inverse of x equals x minus 10'.
Give the student the chance to notice the pattern in the coordinates before telling them that the x and y coordinates swap.
